items.correctExplanation: Yes — your first pick holds the car one-third of the time, so the other closed door carries two-thirds. Switching doubles your odds.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — switch: it wins two-thirds. Your door keeps its original one-third; the host's reveal concentrates the rest onto the other door.
items.lessonContent:
The host's forced reveal moves probability — it never splits it evenly.
Your first pick freezes at one-third the moment you choose.
Information with rules behind it is worth real money.
Share this: run ten penny-cup trials and watch switchers win.
items.question: Three doors, one car. You pick door 1; the host, who knows all, opens door 3 showing a goat. Switch or stay?
items.title: The Classic Switch

items.correctExplanation: Right — your door keeps its 1% while the host's 98 reveals pile 99% onto the survivor. Scale makes the logic undeniable.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, switch: 99% wins. Your first pick is almost surely wrong, and the host just eliminated every alternative but one.
items.lessonContent:
Scaling a puzzle to a hundred doors exposes the mechanism.
Your pick stays 1-in-100 no matter what opens elsewhere.
When intuition rebels, scale the numbers until it surrenders.
Share this: explain the hundred-door version to a skeptic.
items.question: One hundred doors, one car. You pick one; the host opens 98 goat doors. Switch to the survivor?
items.title: The Ninety-Eight Goats

items.correctExplanation: Correct — ten doors mean your pick is 10% and the nine others share 90%, all landing on the survivor. Switching wins nine times in ten.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Switch: 90% wins. Your door's 10% never grew; the host funneled the other 90% onto a single door.
items.lessonContent:
Reveals concentrate probability the way lenses focus light.
Count what your door held at the start — that never changes.
Forecasting who gains from news is a tradeable skill.
Share this: deal ten cards and play host for a friend.
items.question: Ten chests, one treasure. You choose one; the host opens 8 empty chests. Switch to the last closed chest?
items.title: The Ten Chests

items.correctExplanation: Yes — staying holds 25% while the 75% remainder splits across two doors at 37.5% each. Switching to either still beats staying.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — switch: 37.5% beats 25%. One reveal can't carry the whole remainder onto one door when two remain.
items.lessonContent:
Leftover probability splits among ALL survivors, not your favorite.
Count the survivors before crowning a winner.
Partial reveals give partial edges — take them anyway.
Share this: split a remainder fairly across survivors once today.
items.question: Four doors, one car. You pick one; the host opens one goat door. Two others remain. Your best move?
items.title: The Fourth Door

items.correctExplanation: Exactly — a clueless host reveals nothing, so the two doors stand truly equal. Knowledge, not ceremony, moves the odds.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — no gain: genuinely fifty-fifty. The host stumbled onto a goat blindly, so no information entered the game.
items.lessonContent:
Only informed reveals move probability; accidents move nothing.
Ask what the revealer knew before updating your odds.
Luck that looks like news is still just luck.
Share this: separate one informed signal from one lucky accident.
items.question: The host forgot where the car is, opened a random door, and luckily showed a goat. Switch or stay?
items.title: The Forgetful Host

items.correctAnswer: No advantage — one in three anywhere
items.correctExplanation: Right — a reveal before your pick informs nobody. All three doors still hold one-third each, including the opened... the two closed ones.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, no advantage: one in three anywhere. Information must arrive after your commitment to favor anyone.
items.lessonContent:
Timing decides whether news is useful or decoration.
Early reveals help everyone equally, which means no one.
Commit first, then let information work for you.
Share this: notice one decision where order decided everything.
items.question: The host opens a goat door BEFORE you choose. Does any door now beat the others?
items.title: The Premature Peek
choices: No advantage — one in three anywhere

items.correctExplanation: Correct — with no reveal, switching just trades one one-third door for another. Ceremony without information changes nothing.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Indifferent: still one in three. Nobody learned anything, so the swap is pure theater.
items.lessonContent:
No news means no edge — demand the reveal before moving.
Rituals feel strategic while changing zero odds.
Patience beats motion when information is missing.
Share this: skip one purposeless switch today and smile.
items.question: You pick a door; the host opens nothing but offers a swap. Should you?
items.title: The Empty Offer

items.correctExplanation: Yes — an adversary who places the prize to punish switchers flips the math. Assumptions about the host ARE the math.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — stay: the game is rigged. If placement reacts to your strategy, the classic numbers no longer apply.
items.lessonContent:
Every probability answer sits on assumptions — audit them first.
'Random placement' is a load-bearing claim, not décor.
Rigged games punish textbook play on purpose.
Share this: name one hidden assumption behind a famous answer.
items.question: The host watches your pick, then slides the car behind a door to defeat switchers. Now what?
items.title: The Rigged Stage

items.correctExplanation: Exactly — the newcomer shares no history with either door. Information is personal: yours moved your odds, not theirs.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — fifty-fifty for the newcomer. They never made a first pick, so the reveal concentrated nothing for them.
items.lessonContent:
Probability follows the observer, not the furniture.
Two people can rationally hold different odds about one door.
Ask whose history a number belongs to before borrowing it.
Share this: explain why latecomers face fresh odds.
items.question: After the classic reveal, a newcomer who saw nothing picks between the two closed doors. Their odds?
items.title: The Late Arrival

items.correctExplanation: Right — having watched your pick and the reveal, the friend inherits the full situation. Knowledge transfers by watching, not by touching.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, switch: the watcher knows. They saw the original pick and the forced reveal, so the two-thirds sits on the same door for them.
items.lessonContent:
Watching a random process can grant the player's edge.
Information travels with attention, not participation.
Spectators with full history bet like insiders.
Share this: learn one game fully by watching before playing.
items.question: Your friend watched your pick and the host's reveal, then takes over your choice. What should they do?
items.title: The Watching Friend

items.correctAnswer: A stays one-third; C rises to two-thirds
items.correctExplanation: Correct — naming B sacrifices B's third to C, never to A. A's pardon chance never moved; C inherits the freed probability.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! A stays one-third while C rises to two-thirds. The warden's news spends B's share entirely on C.
items.lessonContent:
News about others reallocates their share, never yours.
Prisoners, doors, and envelopes all obey this conservation.
Track whose slice the news spends before celebrating.
Share this: retell the three-prisoners twist at dinner.
items.question: Prisoners A, B, C await fate; one is pardoned. The warden tells A that B will die. What are A's vs C's chances now?
items.title: The Warden's Whisper
choices: A stays one-third; C rises to two-thirds

items.correctAnswer: Two-thirds — the other drawer is gold
items.correctExplanation: Yes — three gold drawers against three silver mean a gold draw points to the double-gold box two-thirds of the time. Draws sample drawers, not boxes.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — two-thirds: the other drawer is gold. Gold drawers cluster in the double-gold box, weighting the odds.
items.lessonContent:
Samples come from drawers, and rich boxes hold more of them.
Counting containers instead of contents is the classic slip.
Weight every hypothesis by how many draws it supplies.
Share this: demo the three-box paradox with coins.
items.question: Boxes hold gold-gold, silver-silver, gold-silver. A drawn drawer shows gold. How likely is the other drawer gold?
items.title: The Golden Drawer
choices: Two-thirds — the other drawer is gold

items.correctExplanation: Right — staying keeps 20% while the 80% remainder splits over two survivors at 40% each. Either switch doubles your fate.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, switch: 40% beats 20%. Two reveals leave two doors sharing the 80% your pick never held.
items.lessonContent:
Multiple reveals still obey one conservation law.
Your pick's share never grows; survivors divide the rest.
Bigger casts shrink individual shares but keep the rule.
Share this: compute one five-door split by hand.
items.question: Five sealed envelopes hold one prize ticket. Yours is marked; the host tears open two losing envelopes. Move your claim to a survivor?
items.title: The Five Doors

items.correctExplanation: Exactly — one pick holds 25% and two reveals pile the other 75% onto the last door. Two reveals, one jackpot door.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Switch: 75% wins. Your quarter never budged while the host swept three-quarters onto a single door.
items.lessonContent:
Each reveal sweeps more of the field onto the survivor.
Late survivors carry the weight of every opened door.
Let the host's labor work for you — then take it.
Share this: feel 75% land on one door and grin.
items.question: Four caskets hide one gem. After your claim, the host lifts two empty lids, leaving a single rival casket. Take it?
items.title: The Double Reveal

items.correctExplanation: Correct — every door starts equal, so door 1 and a dice-picked door both hold one-third. Rituals can't bend symmetry.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — no difference: symmetry protects you. No door outranks another before the reveal, however chosen.
items.lessonContent:
Symmetric choices are interchangeable — pick fast and move on.
Superstition taxes the indecisive with wasted rituals.
Save deliberation for asymmetric decisions.
Share this: pick one trivial choice by dice today.
items.question: Does always picking door 1 beat picking randomly each show?
items.title: The Lucky Number

items.correctExplanation: Yes — a host who opens only for winners just announced your victory. The reveal itself is the message; read it.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — stay: opening confesses your win. This host's policy turns every reveal into a winner's certificate.
items.lessonContent:
Policies leak through actions — decode the policy, not the move.
A reveal conditioned on your success announces it.
Ask why THIS move happened now before reacting.
Share this: read one policy hidden inside one action.
items.question: This host opens a door ONLY when you first picked the car. A door opens. Now what?
items.title: The Strange Host

items.correctExplanation: Right — a host who opens only for losers just announced your defeat. Flee the losing door while flight is offered.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, switch: opening confesses your loss. The policy guarantees your pick is wrong whenever a reveal occurs.
items.lessonContent:
Conditioned reveals are confessions wearing stage makeup.
Losers get curtains; winners get silence — learn the grammar.
Meta-rules about behavior outrank the behavior itself.
Share this: spot one rule that flips the obvious move.
items.question: At this table the curtain rises only to mock a losing first pick. Tonight it rises. Where is the car?
items.title: The Cruel Host

items.correctExplanation: Correct — 'two doors left' ignores HOW one left. The forced reveal funneled two-thirds onto the survivor; counting doors erases that history.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Wrong: history concentrates the odds. Two survivors are not two equals when one inherited the opened door's share.
items.lessonContent:
'Two options' never implies 'fifty-fifty' — ask about their pasts.
Equal counts with unequal histories deceive everywhere.
Resumes matter more than headcounts in odds and hiring.
Share this: kill one fifty-fifty myth with its backstory.
items.question: 'Two doors remain, so it must be fifty-fifty.' What is wrong with that?
items.title: The Fifty Fallacy

items.correctExplanation: Yes — simulation sides with switching about two times in three. Frequencies confirm the fractions; run it yourself.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — about 667 switcher wins. A thousand simulated shows let the two-thirds emerge from noise.
items.lessonContent:
Simulations settle bar bets that algebra cannot.
Code ten lines and watch theory become frequency.
Empiricism is the friend logic deserves.
Share this: simulate one paradox and show a skeptic.
items.question: A computer simulates 1,000 classic shows with always-switch. About how many wins?
items.title: The Thousand Shows

items.correctExplanation: Exactly — switch-losses sting more, so players cling to their doors. Anticipated regret, not math, picks the strategy.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Players stay too often. The extra sting of a failed switch scares contestants into the worse strategy.
items.lessonContent:
Feelings tax rationality — regret aversion costs real money.
Design choices that forgive the better strategy.
Notice when comfort, not calculation, steers you.
Share this: take one right-but-scary switch this week.
items.question: Losing after switching feels worse than losing after staying. What does that predict?
items.title: The Sting Study

items.correctExplanation: Right — with door 1 doubly likely, a reveal elsewhere concentrates even harder: switching to door 1 wins four times in five. Priors amplify the edge.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, switch: now 80%. The loaded prior plus the reveal stack together, pushing the survivor past the classic two-thirds.
items.lessonContent:
Unequal priors stack with reveals instead of canceling.
Update in order: prior first, evidence second.
Loaded dice and loaded doors obey one update rule.
Share this: update one belief twice — prior, then news.
items.question: The car sits behind door 1 twice as often as elsewhere. You pick door 2; the host opens door 3 (goat). Switch to door 1?
items.title: The Loaded Stage

items.correctExplanation: Correct — switching wins a $10,000 car two-thirds of the time: about $6,667 of expectation against $4,000 cash. The math declines politely.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! Refuse: switching beats the cash. Two-thirds of ten thousand outweighs four thousand certain — take the odds, not the bribe.
items.lessonContent:
Price every offer against expectation, not excitement.
Certainty seduces; arithmetic decides.
Game shows monetize your fear of variance.
Share this: compute one expectation before accepting one offer.
items.question: Car worth $10,000. After the reveal, the host offers $4,000 cash to walk away. Take it?
items.title: The Cash Temptation

items.correctExplanation: Yes — shuffling re-randomizes the car between the two doors. Information destroyed is probability reset.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — fifty-fifty: shuffling erases history. The car now sits randomly behind either door, and the reveal's work is undone.
items.lessonContent:
Randomization destroys information as surely as fire destroys paper.
Shuffles, redraws, and resets return odds to flat.
Guard information — it evaporates on disturbance.
Share this: name one shuffle that reset somebody's edge.
items.question: After the classic reveal, the host shuffles the car randomly behind the two closed doors. Now what?
items.title: The Great Shuffle

items.correctExplanation: Right — switch then switch-back equals never moving: one-third. The extra ceremony can't launder the odds.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, decline: switching back is staying. Two swaps return you to the original one-third door, not to safety.
items.lessonContent:
Round trips return you to the original odds, not better ones.
Motion feels like progress while arithmetic naps.
Count net movement, not total movement.
Share this: catch one double-move that returns to start.
items.question: You switched to the survivor. The host offers to switch you BACK for $100. Accept?
items.title: The Return Ticket

items.correctAnswer: One in three — others change nothing
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — rivals' picks are decoration on your one-third. Only reveals move odds; company merely watches.
items.incorrectExplanation: Close! One in three: others change nothing. Their doors hold their own thirds, and no reveal has moved a single point.
items.lessonContent:
Crowds don't dilute your share without new information.
Independence means neighbors' picks never touch yours.
Envy of others' doors is probability illiteracy.
Share this: hold your door calmly in a crowded game.
items.question: Three contestants each pick a different door; no reveal happens. What are your winning odds?
items.title: The Crowded Stage
choices: One in three — others change nothing
